item.title: Zurich approves stricter regulations for skyscrapers
item.description: Zurich approved the stricter variant of the zoning plan with 62,6% of the vote and a turnout of 45,8%, while the city has around 300 buildings taller than 25 meters.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Zurich restricts areas for skyscrapers - 62.6% approve the stricter variant - 62.6% reject the Municipal Council's counter-proposal - Voter turnout: 45.8%
## Key Facts - What → partial revision of the BZO zoning plan - Where → city of Zurich - Tall buildings → approximately 300 over 25 meters - Buildings up to 80 meters → railway tracks and Oerlikon center - Vote → 62.6% for the City Council's variant - Turnout → 45.8%
Zurich has approved the partial revision of the zoning plan, the Bau- und Zonenordnung (BZO), in a vote, introducing a stricter framework for skyscrapers and reducing the areas in which they can be built. The news was reported by Keystone-ATS.
Currently, the city has approximately 300 buildings taller than 25 meters. This figure provides the background for a revision that the Municipal Council had presented with a less restrictive approach than the one later approved by the City Council.
The initial project planned to keep the total area designated for residential towers virtually unchanged. The executive branch wanted to reduce the zones for buildings up to 80 meters, introduce new areas for those up to 60 meters, and expand the areas for constructions between 25 and 40 meters.
### The variant chosen at the polls
The City Council profoundly modified the project. In the approved variant, buildings up to 80 meters will be permitted only along railway tracks and in the center of Oerlikon. Furthermore, several zones planned for constructions up to 40 meters were eliminated.
For the left and the SVP, this solution makes it possible to avoid a wave of demolitions and to better protect the population from the risk of displacement from their neighborhoods. The stated objective for both variants remained the integration of tall buildings into the urban fabric. The plan indicated directions such as more lively ground floors, more space for public and community use, and an enhancement of green areas.
The outcome of the vote gave 62.6% to the more restrictive variant of the City Council. The Municipal Council's counter-proposal was rejected by the same percentage. Turnout was 45.8%. The vote therefore chose the project modified by the City Council, not the initial proposal from the Municipal Council. ## The practical significance for the city
The practical significance of the vote lies in the selection of locations, not in a new abstract height category. A comparison of the two projects shows that the municipal government had envisaged a redistribution of the areas: less space for buildings up to 80 metres, new areas for buildings up to 60 metres and an expansion for constructions between 25 and 40 metres. The City Council pushed the restriction further, limiting buildings up to 80 metres to the railway tracks and the centre of Oerlikon and eliminating several zones for those up to 40 metres.
For Swiss readers, the case brings together four housing issues in a single vote: where to build, how high, how to integrate ground floors and how to enhance green spaces and community uses.
### Before and after, without confusing the variants
| Element | Municipal government's proposal | Approved variant | |---|---|---| | Buildings up to 80 metres | Reduction of the zones | Only along the railway tracks and in the centre of Oerlikon | | Constructions between 25 and 40 metres | Expansion of the areas | Several zones eliminated |
For those living in the city, this distinction offers a practical key to understanding the issue. The question is not only how tall a building can be, but in which area it can be placed. For the up-to-80-metre range, the answer contained in the approved variant is limited to two territorial references: the railway tracks and the centre of Oerlikon. For the range between 25 and 40 metres, by contrast, the source notes the elimination of several zones that the initial project would have expanded.
The vote therefore links vertical development to the shape of everyday spaces. Both variants aimed for livelier ground floors, more space for public and community uses and the enhancement of green areas. These are the elements to observe when assessing the result from an urban perspective: not only the presence of a tall building, but the relationship between construction, the street level, collective uses and greenery.
The reference to the railway tracks makes it natural to pair the urban-planning perspective with that of the mezzi pubblici. For Swiss readers, the case shows how density, neighbourhoods, collective spaces and greenery are connected in the debate. The arguments of the left and the SVP remain central: avoiding a wave of demolitions and providing greater protection for the population against the risk of being displaced from their neighbourhoods.

item.title: Physiotherapy in Ticino: moratorium is not enough, Physioswiss
item.description: In Ticino, outpatient physiotherapy is growing; reimbursements per insured person increased by 42% between 2017 and 2023, and the SUPSI study was delivered in May 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Outpatient physiotherapy is growing in Ticino - Reimbursements per insured person rose by 42% between 2017 and 2023 - The SUPSI study was delivered in May 2026 - Physioswiss proposes a register to the DSS
## Key facts What → growth of outpatient physiotherapy in Ticino Who → Physioswiss Ticino Study → commissioned from SUPSI's DEASS Location → Bioggio Period → particularly marked increase in Ticino since 2020 Swiss data → reimbursements for physiotherapy per insured person rose by 42% between 2017 and 2023 Training → 32 SUPSI places; 120 in Italian and 120 in French at Campus LUDES Proposal → register of active healthcare personnel, censuses and checks
In Bioggio, in May 2026, Physioswiss Ticino presented an independent study commissioned from SUPSI's DEASS and delivered that same month. The research argues that outpatient physiotherapy is growing in Ticino, but that limiting new authorizations to independent practice would not be sufficient to manage the phenomenon.
The analysis confirms a significant increase in consumption and expenditure borne by compulsory insurance, particularly marked in Ticino since 2020. However, the phenomenon concerns the whole of Switzerland: between 2017 and 2023, reimbursements for physiotherapy per insured person rose by 42%. The reasons cited include shorter hospital stays, care at home, separate billing in nursing homes and greater use of medical prescriptions. The study also considers the gradual shift from hospital to outpatient care.
### Authorizations, training and checks
According to Physioswiss, a moratorium on new authorizations would not prevent existing facilities from hiring employed physiotherapists. The same problem would affect new graduates and could encourage market concentration.
The study highlights the importance of training. In addition to SUPSI's 32 places, Campus LUDES offers 120 places each year in Ticino for a bachelor's degree in Italian and the same number in French. The qualification is issued by a foreign university and subsequently recognized in Switzerland.
SUPSI also identified some critical issues: active professionals who are not registered in the national register of healthcare professions; offerings that combine fitness and gym services with services reimbursed by health insurers; business models that present physiotherapy as a highly profitable investment.
For Physioswiss, what is primarily lacking is a precise picture of the sector. It is not known how many physiotherapists are actually active in Ticino or at what level of employment. The association therefore proposes to the DSS a register of active healthcare personnel, censuses, systematic checks of registrations, more effective quality criteria and a clear distinction between healthcare services and fitness.
> «We are not asking for preferential treatment. We are asking that the measures target the real problems», says president Tamara Roncati. ## Why a moratorium is not enough to capture the sector
A moratorium applied to new authorizations for independent practice would target a specific point, but on its own would not measure the actual presence of professionals. Existing facilities can hire employed physiotherapists; therefore, the number of authorizations would not necessarily correspond to the number of active professionals or to their employment rate. This distinction is what makes the register proposed by Physioswiss central.
### Three levels for assessing the impact
| Level | What to observe | Limitation or need identified | |---|---|---| | Authorizations | new independent practices | the moratorium does not cover hiring in existing facilities | | Personnel | active physiotherapists and employment rate | a precise snapshot is currently lacking | | Services | healthcare, fitness and gym | a clear distinction and more incisive quality criteria are needed |
The practical picture also changes for those entering the profession. A new graduate is not only faced with the possibility of obtaining an authorization: they may find themselves in a market where existing facilities continue to hire. The study thus points to a possible shift in growth toward existing operators, with the risk of greater concentration.
The second level concerns reimbursements. The 42% recorded between 2017 and 2023 is calculated per insured person and concerns the whole of Switzerland. The figure must be read together with consumption, expenditure covered by compulsory insurance and the factors identified to explain the growth: shorter hospital stays, continued care at home, separate billing in nursing homes and greater reliance on medical prescriptions.
A more precise database would therefore serve to separate the issue of quantity from that of the appropriateness of care. Monitoring registrations addresses a different aspect from the distinction between healthcare services and fitness; quality criteria add a further level. Anyone assessing a professional placement can consider these questions alongside consulting annunci di lavoro: what form of activity is being offered and how is the service described?
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## An operational framework for the DSS and the sector
The dossier sets out a sequence of checks concerning the DSS. For those who work, study or follow physiotherapy in Switzerland, the order helps distinguish the issue of authorizations from that of the actual presence of personnel, quality and the distinction between healthcare and fitness.
### Five steps to keep distinct
First step: separate independent practice from employed work in existing facilities. This is the boundary that makes it possible to understand what a moratorium would affect and what would remain outside its scope.
Second step: take stock of the active healthcare personnel. The register proposed by Physioswiss should make clear the number of physiotherapists actually active in Ticino and their employment level, two pieces of information that the association currently considers missing.
Third step: systematically check registrations in the national register of healthcare professions. The verification addresses the issue identified by SUPSI concerning active professionals who are not registered.
Fourth step: distinguish healthcare services from fitness and gym activities. The separation serves to clarify which offerings are presented together with services reimbursed by health insurance funds and which belong to a commercial model.
Fifth step: apply more incisive quality criteria and assess the appropriateness of care. From Physioswiss's perspective, growth should be managed with data, quality and appropriateness, taking into account the gradual shift from hospital to outpatient care.
For those following the sector, this framework makes it possible to examine upcoming measures without confusing authorizations, employment and training. Training should be kept separate from the employment count: the study indicates the 32 places at SUPSI and the places proposed by Campus LUDES in Italian and French, while Physioswiss is also calling for a census of the personnel actually active.
The criterion indicated by the association remains to manage growth on the basis of data, quality and appropriateness of care. To explore the economic side of work in Switzerland, use the calcolatore stipendio.

item.title: Upper Engadine Healthcare: agreements approved through 2029
item.description: The vote of the eleven Municipalities ensures almost 28.5 million francs for the Samedan hospital, elderly homes, Spitex and the Sanadura entity from 2027 to 2029.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 42% of those entitled to vote went to the polls - Almost 90% approved the four agreements - In every municipality, the yes vote reached at least 80% - Almost 28,5 million francs through 2029
## Key facts - Turnout → 42% of those entitled to vote - Overall approval → almost 90% - Minimum approval in municipalities → 80% - Duration → from 2027 to 2029 - Samedan Hospital → 16,9 million francs - Nursing homes → 9,9 million francs - Spitex service → 490’000 francs - Sanadura management → 1,2 million francs
42% of those entitled to vote in the eleven municipalities of the Upper Engadine took part in the consultation on regional healthcare. Almost 90% approved the four new service agreements with the Sanadura management body, Samedan Hospital, the nursing homes and the Spitex service. In no locality did support fall below 80%.
The vote ensures the continuity of healthcare in the Upper Engadine for the next three years. The agreements cover the period from 2027 to 2029 and, according to the source, offer healthcare providers greater certainty for planning the future. The result comes after a phase in which the future and financing of healthcare provision were submitted several times to the judgment of those entitled to vote.
### The package worth almost 28,5 million
The overall package amounts to almost 28,5 million francs. 16,9 million over three years is earmarked for Samedan Hospital; 9,9 million is allocated to the nursing homes, while 490’000 francs are provided for the Spitex service. A further 1,2 million is provided for the management of the Sanadura body. The result therefore brings the hospital, facilities for the elderly, Spitex care and the management body into the same framework, with separate amounts but a common duration.
### Services unchanged in Samedan
At the Samedan facility, services will remain as they are today. The provision includes 24-hour emergency care throughout the year, surgery, gynaecology and obstetrics, paediatrics, internal medicine and a semi-intensive care unit. Specialist outpatient services are also planned, as are specialist consultations for dialysis, gastroenterology and oncology, in addition to basic care for emergency and scheduled treatments.
Over the next three years, Sanadura wants to increase bed occupancy, with an expected benefit for the profitability of the infrastructure in St. Moritz and Samedan. The challenge identified by Sanadura Health Council President Isabel Wenger remains the recruitment of qualified healthcare staff.
> «Today's result represents a strong sign of confidence in healthcare and means that it can now continue its work. It is also excellent news for the population, guests and staff of the healthcare facilities», Wenger told Keystone-ATS. ## Comparison with the previous stages
The practical significance of the vote emerges from comparison with the previous stages, not only from the final result. Since April 2025, eligible voters in the eleven municipalities have been called to the polls four times to decide the future and financing of regional healthcare provision. The current decision comes after two rejections and after an agreement approved in spring, valid until the end of 2026.
### A different outlook from previous attempts
The first vote rejected the merger with the Ospedale cantonale di Coira. In November, a second rescue attempt was rejected, based on a two-year performance agreement and a cost of nearly 51 million francs. The third vote, held in spring, instead led to the creation of the Sanadura management entity and a performance agreement amounting to 19,5 million francs until the end of 2026.
The new package covers three years and amounts to almost 28,5 million francs. Comparison with the previous proposal therefore shows a longer duration and a different total amount, without requiring further calculations beyond the reported data. Previous votes were repeatedly compared to a bailout because Samedan hospital was drowning in debt. Wenger describes the new outlook as more stable, with funding and services clearly regulated.
### A service chain with distinct responsibilities
Sanadura is a public-law entity active since April 1, 2026. Its operating model does not concentrate all services in the same way:
| Area | Structure indicated by the source | |---|---| | Sanadura | Provides services directly or purchases them from third parties | | Nursing homes | Are managed by Sanadura | | Hospital services | Are guaranteed through a contract with Spital Oberengadin | | Spital Oberengadin | Is part of the Ospedale cantonale di Coira group |
This distinction helps interpret the funding together with the organization. The Board of Directors, composed of seven people and chaired by Michael Rolaz, is responsible for strategic leadership and healthcare management. The Health Council, by contrast, brings together eleven people, one from each municipality, with political and strategic responsibilities.
At the operational level, the source identifies two variables to monitor: increased bed occupancy, linked to the profitability of the facilities in St. Moritz and Samedan, and the ability to find qualified healthcare staff. Those wishing to monitor employment can consult annunci di lavoro, keeping this issue distinct from the decision on the contracts.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## How to follow the dossier
To track the decision effectively, it is best to turn the material into a checklist. The procedure adheres strictly to the dates, amounts, and responsibilities indicated by the source.
### Four steps to interpret the decision
1. **Set the reference period.** Separate the agreements valid from 2027 to 2029 from the previous agreement, around 19.5 million francs, valid until the end of 2026. This keeps each figure tied to its respective phase.
2. Match the content to the facility. Distinguish between the Samedan hospital, nursing homes, the Spitex service, and Sanadura management. For the hospital, also note that the specified services include both emergency and scheduled treatments.
3. Reconstruct responsibility. Verify whether the service is provided directly by Sanadura or purchased from third parties. For the hospital component, the stated organizational reference is the contract with Spital Oberengadin; for nursing homes, management is directly assigned to Sanadura.
4. Note the two operational indicators. The source links the next three years to the goal of increasing bed occupancy and highlights the recruitment of qualified healthcare personnel as a challenge. These are the two elements to keep separate when assessing the development of the facilities.
On the financial sheet, amounts should be listed next to their respective agreement: 16.9 million francs for the Samedan hospital, 9.9 million for nursing homes, 490,000 francs for Spitex, and 1.2 million for Sanadura management. The total indicated by the source is nearly 28.5 million francs. It is best not to add items not mentioned by the source or turn the overall package into an individual expense.
To complete the overview, also note the governance: Sanadura will be operational from April 1, 2026, with a Board of Directors of seven members and a Healthcare Council of eleven, one per municipality. For the general healthcare framework, consult LAMal/health insurance. To link professional planning to your income, use the salary calculator.

item.title: Zurich, yes to assisted suicide in healthcare facilities
item.description: In Zurich, 68,1% approve assisted suicide in healthcare facilities. Turnout 47,6%; the law on teachers was rejected by 59,2%.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- In Zurich, 68,1% approve the new law - Voter turnout: 47,6% - Psychiatric facilities and prisons excluded - 59,2% reject the teachers' law
## Key facts
- Outcome on the healthcare law → 68,1% yes - Turnout → 47,6% - Outcome on the teachers' law → 59,2% no - Requirement provided for → nursing homes, care facilities, hospitals and rehabilitation clinics - Excluded → psychiatric facilities and prisons - Counterproposal → popular initiative meanwhile withdrawn - Cost feared by municipalities and cities → 83 million francs - Estimated share borne by them → around 67 million francs
In Zurich, 68,1% approved the law requiring nursing homes, care facilities, hospitals and rehabilitation clinics to allow assisted suicide within their walls. Turnout was 47,6%. Keystone-ATS reports this.
The reform had been drafted by the Grand Council as a counterproposal to a popular initiative that was subsequently withdrawn. The text was contested by a bourgeois minority and by the Cantonal Council. The latter supported extending the requirement to nursing homes and care facilities, but opposed also imposing it on hospitals and rehabilitation clinics.
### The scope of the approved law
The result therefore defines a precise scope. Psychiatric facilities and prisons are excluded from the reform. The situation indicated before the vote provided for the requirement only for nursing and care homes managed by the municipalities or on their behalf. The passage approved in Zurich adds hospitals and rehabilitation clinics, in the text described by the source, among the facilities required to allow assisted suicide.
The Zurich ballot also included a second law, dedicated to teachers' working conditions. The proposal was rejected by 59,2% of voters. For teachers responsible for classes, the annual hours allocated to additional activities would have risen from 100 to 160, including meetings with parents and the organization of school trips. The lesson factor would have risen from 58 to 59, with more paid time for preparation.
The education reform was supported by the teachers' association, but opposed by 99 municipalities and cities, backed by UDC and PLR. Their objection concerned additional costs of 83 million francs, of which around 67 million would have been borne by them. For the section concerning paid time, the reader can compare the news with the practical guide on busta paga svizzera. The practical significance of the Zurich vote emerges from comparing the rule already described with the scope of the approved reform. The decision does not concern every care facility indiscriminately: the source names specific categories and also indicates two exclusions.
| Scope | Situation indicated | |---|---| | Current obligation | Nursing and care homes managed by the municipalities or on their behalf | | Approved text | Nursing homes, care facilities, hospitals and rehabilitation clinics | | Outside the reform | Psychiatric facilities and prisons | | Position of the State Council | Yes to nursing and care homes; no to hospitals and rehabilitation |
The difference between the rows of the table makes it possible to interpret the result without turning it into a general obligation. A municipal nursing home or care facility was already covered by the framework indicated by the source. Hospitals and rehabilitation clinics, on the other hand, represent the extension supported by the approved text, while psychiatric facilities and prisons remain outside it. The State Council had supported a narrower solution: in favor of the first two categories, opposed to including the other two.
The second outcome has a different organizational impact. With 59,2% voting no, the teachers' law did not pass the consultation: the proposal to increase the annual hours of teachers responsible for classes from 100 to 160 for supplementary activities was not accepted, nor was the proposal to increase the lesson factor from 58 to 59. The two figures described a project, not a change approved by the vote.
### The issue of costs for Municipalities and Cities
The source links the opposition of 99 Municipalities and Cities to fears of additional costs of 83 million francs, approximately 67 million of them borne by the municipalities and cities. The teachers' association, on the other hand, supported the reform. This figure makes it possible to distinguish the sphere of teaching work from that of local spending: the former concerned hours, activities and paid preparation; the latter the allocation of the costs feared. For a broader look at everyday expenses in Switzerland, the site offers the guide to costo della vita in Svizzera.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. To read the two results without conflating them, it is advisable to create a separate sheet for the healthcare part and one for the school-related part. The procedure can remain faithful to the published data.
### Sheet for facilities
1. Identify the category: nursing home, care facility, hospital, rehabilitation clinic, psychiatric facility or prison. 2. Compare the category with the previous framework: the obligation indicated by the source applied to nursing homes and care facilities managed by the municipalities or on their behalf. 3. Record the approved text: hospitals and rehabilitation clinics are included; psychiatric facilities and prisons remain excluded. 4. Separate this verification from the position of the Council of State, which advocated extending it only to nursing homes and care facilities.
### Sheet for schools and municipalities
Here, the first figure to record is the 59,2% voting no. The figures 100 and 160 concerned the annual hours of class teachers for supplementary activities; 58 and 59 were the assumed values for the lesson factor. They are therefore the figures from the rejected proposal, to be kept separate from the decision on assisted suicide.
For the local dimension, the sheet must also report the 99 municipalities and cities opposed, the support of UDC and PLR for their position, the feared additional cost of 83 million francs and the share of approximately 67 million borne by them. In this way, the reader separates the organization of school work from the financial argument cited in the source.
The paid-time item can be paired with the guide on busta paga svizzera, already relevant to the school proposal; for a personal simulation of the salary component, use calcolatore stipendio.

item.title: Geneva approves free contraception with 58,5%
item.description: 58,5% of Geneva voters approved free contraception; turnout 44,2%, estimated cost 20 million francs/year, implementation expected in 2028.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Geneva approves free contraception with 58,5% - Voter turnout: 44,2% - Mobility in France: credit approved with 56,8% - Housing: reform rejected with 63,5%
## Key facts - Location → Geneva - Contraception → universal free access, approved by 58,5% of voters - Turnout → 44,2% - Estimated costs → approximately 20 million francs per year - Implementation → 2028 - Mobility → credit of 39,5 million francs; yes vote at 56,8% - Funding → proposed reduction of 2 million francs per year from 2026 - Housing → legislative amendment rejected with 63,5%
### The vote on contraception
Geneva is the first Canton to approve the principle of universal free access to contraception. The Socialist initiative «For free contraception» was approved today by 58,5% of voters. Turnout was 44,2%.
According to Keystone-ATS, all methods whose effectiveness is recognized will be included: the pill, intrauterine devices, also called coils, implants, injections, patches, vaginal rings, the morning-after pill and condoms. Costs are estimated at approximately 20 million francs per year.
During the campaign, the left and the Centre supported the text in the name of equal access to sexual and contraceptive healthcare. PLR, MCG and UDC, together with the Council of State, opposed it instead: in their view, the initiative was not sufficiently targeted at people on low incomes.
The next step is institutional. The ball is now in the Council of State's court, which will have to prepare an implementing law. Health official Pierre Maudet intends to bring together gynecologists, pharmacists, associations and initiative organizers to discuss the scope of the text and the measures to be adopted. Implementation of the initiative is expected in 2028.
### The other decisions at the ballot box
In today's vote, the people of Geneva also approved a credit of 39,5 million francs to co-finance mobility infrastructure in neighboring France: the yes vote reached 56,8%. The project provides for 1600 additional parking spaces at French P+R facilities, priority lanes for buses and an extension of the tram network, with the aim of reducing by 15'000 the number of vehicles that travel on the Canton's roads every day.
With the exception of MCG and UDC, which allowed members to vote freely, all parties had called for approval of the credit.
On another issue, the people of Geneva instead rejected, with 58,5% of the vote, the proposal to reduce by 2 million francs per year, starting in 2026, the funding provided for by the 2025-2028 performance agreement between the University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland and the Canton.
Finally, the legislative amendment aimed at facilitating tenants' purchase of housing was rejected with 63,5%. The Tenants' Association had launched the referendum against the reform because it feared an increase in lease terminations. ## Practical implications for those who live and work in Geneva
### A principle to be turned into rules
The decision on contraception currently produces a political direction, not a complete operational timetable. The approved text enshrines the principle of universal free access; its implementation depends on the law that the Council of State still has to prepare. For those living in the Canton, the distinction is concrete: the ballot outcome clarifies the direction, while the next phase will have to specify the scope and the measures to be adopted. The round table announced by Pierre Maudet with gynecologists, pharmacists, associations and initiative proponents is the indicated step for discussing implementation, but the vote does not yet describe an individual procedure for obtaining free access.
The annual estimate makes the financial dimension of the choice visible. It is not, however, an individual figure: it is associated with the overall implementation of the measure. To read this figure alongside other family expenses, the site provides costo della vita in Svizzera. The contrast that emerged during the campaign also points to something to monitor: on the one hand, universal access; on the other, the request to focus the intervention on people with low incomes.
### Mobility, education and housing
The credit for infrastructure in neighboring France has a practical impact linked to travel, but the project brings together different instruments: P+R car parks, preferential lanes for buses and a tram network. The stated objective is to reduce traffic on cantonal roads. Those who travel every day will therefore have to distinguish the vote on funding from the concrete implementation of individual projects: the source does not indicate a timetable for their becoming operational.
The other two no votes concern choices with different effects. The rejection of the proposed reduction in funding for the University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland should not be read as approval of a new expenditure: the vote rejected that cut. The legislative amendment on tenants' purchase of their housing, on the other hand, was not approved; the referendum had been promoted by the Tenants' Association out of fear of an increase in terminations. For the other Cantons, the point to retain is the cantonal nature of the decisions: the source describes the Geneva vote and does not automatically announce the same measures elsewhere.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## How to follow implementation
### Three steps for the healthcare dossier
1. Separate the outcome from the mechanism. The vote approves the principle of universal free provision; the step to follow is the implementing law of the Council of State. Until that text is defined, do not attribute to the decision a request channel, a payment method or a procedure that the source does not indicate.
2. Check the scope of the law. The discussion announced by Pierre Maudet will bring together gynecologists, pharmacists, associations and initiative supporters. To follow the dossier, verify how the text will translate the list of recognized methods and what measures will be adopted. Implementation is expected in 2028: this is the political deadline indicated by the source.
3. Keep the overall estimate separate from the personal one. The annual estimate concerns the initiative as a whole and does not, on its own, constitute the amount attributed to an individual person. An individual calculation would require implementing rules that the vote does not yet provide.
### A framework for the other results
For mobility, follow separately the three elements of the approved project: new spaces in French P+R facilities, priority lanes for buses and extension of the tram network. The objective regarding vehicles is indicated by the source, but is not accompanied by an operational timetable; therefore, it is advisable not to set personal dates based solely on the vote. Anyone who uses mezzi pubblici can use these three items as a reference for reading subsequent updates.
For education, note that the proposal to reduce funding during the specified contractual period was rejected: it should not be described as an approved reduction. For housing, the amendment that would have facilitated purchase by tenants was rejected; the result does not authorize treating it as a new rule.
The scope remains Geneva-specific. Anyone living in another Canton must not turn Geneva's vote into a national measure. To connect these decisions to your monthly budget, use calcolatore stipendio.

item.title: Air defense: evaluation of Bodluv GR 2 completed
item.description: Armasuisse has completed the evaluation for the second Bodluv GR 2 ground-to-air defense system. The choice goes to the Federal Council.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Evaluation concluded for the second Bodluv GR 2 system - Choice of model goes to the Federal Council - The Patriot will be delayed by five to seven years - 5 billion francs are earmarked for the second system
## Key facts
- Subject → second ground-based air defense system - Internal name → Bodluv GR 2 - Decision → Federal Council - Patriot delay → five to seven years - Realistic delivery → by 2032 - Bids → France, Israel and South Korea - Possible winner according to SonntagsBlick → Eurosam - Additional army funding → 24 billion francs
### The evaluation phase closes
The Federal Office for Defence Procurement, Armasuisse, has completed the evaluation of the second ground-based air defense system intended for the Swiss Army. item.description: The Swiss people reject the proposal to increase self-sufficiency to 70% in ten years. All the cantons voted against it.

## In brief - 72,5% no: food initiative rejected - All cantons voted against - Voter turnout: 47,03% - Objective: 70% self-sufficiency in ten years
## Key facts - Outcome → 72,5% no - Voter turnout → 47,03% - Final poll → 64% no - Filing → 16 agosto 2024 - Valid signatures → 112’736 - Self-sufficiency → from the current 45% to at least 70% in ten years - Promoters → Franziska Herren and six other people - Cantons → all opposed
With 72,5% voting no, the Swiss people rejected the food initiative. All cantons voted against it; voter turnout was 47,03%. The last poll before the vote indicated 64% opposition.
### A national result, with local differences
In Ticino, the text was rejected by 68,66%, one of the lowest shares; in Grisons, opponents reached 75,01%. The no vote exceeded 80% in Uri (80,82%), Schwyz (81,02%), Appenzell Innerrhoden (80,29%) and Obwalden (80,26%). Nidwalden reached 79,85%. The lowest rejection rates were in Geneva (62,63%), Basel-Stadt (63,16%) and Neuchâtel (65,49%). Verzasca and Campo Vallemaggia, in Ticino, instead accepted the initiative.
The proposal, filed on 16 agosto 2024 with 112’736 valid signatures, was titled «For a secure food supply – by strengthening sustainable domestic production, more plant-based foodstuffs and clean drinking water (Food Initiative)». It called for significantly greater agricultural production to reduce dependence on foreign countries and increase food security. The text aimed to shift consumption and production towards plant-based foods, protect the environment and water, and increase net self-sufficiency from the current 45% to at least 70% within ten years.
Behind the text were Franziska Herren, from the association «Clean Water for All», and six other people. Lukas Golder, a political scientist who spoke on SRF, judged the issues interesting but the implementation too rapid and radical. The committee conducted the campaign largely on its own: Greenpeace Switzerland and the Greens left voters free to choose, while all other parties recommended voting no.
Herren reminded Keystone-ATS that the problems remain and also attributed the defeat to disinformation. «We did not want any menu imposed by the state», she said, explaining that 70% was a target, not a rigid constraint. Markus Ritter, of The Centre and president of the Swiss Farmers’ Union, considered the Federal Council’s goal of bringing self-sufficiency to 50% by 2050 realistic. The Keystone-ATS report completes the picture of a vote without the structural change expected for agriculture over the next ten years. ## What the vote indicates
### A rejection of the requirement, not of the issues
The vote blocks the proposal to turn into a constitutional requirement a fast-track approach: more domestic production, more plant-based foods, protection of the environment and water, and net self-sufficiency at 70% within ten years. The source does not, however, describe an abandonment of the issues, but rather a disagreement over instruments, timing and the degree of obligation.
For the Greens, ecological agricultural policy is not swept away by the no vote; the scorching summer with worrying records cited by the party shows the need for more ecological agriculture. The PVL separated rejection of the rigid threshold from rejection of healthy soils, clean water and sustainable agriculture.

Economiesuisse interpreted the no vote as a rejection of heavy state intervention; the USAM also regarded it as a signal against state paternalism in other sectors. item.title: Zug, 25 years ago the massacre in the Parliament chamber
item.description: On September 27, 2001, Friedrich Leibacher killed 14 people and wounded 15 in the Zug Parliament, firing 91 shots in 2 minutes and 34 seconds, leading to a change in security.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - September 27, 2001: 14 deaths in the Zug Parliament - Friedrich Leibacher fired 91 shots in 2 minutes and 34 seconds - Three State Councillors and 11 deputies were killed - The massacre changed the protection of Swiss parliaments
## Key facts - Date → September 27, 2001 - Location → Grand Council of Zug chamber - Perpetrator → Friedrich Leibacher - Victims → 14 people - Injured → 15 people - Shots fired → 91 - Attack duration → 2 minutes and 34 seconds - First aid → 10:45 AM
On September 27, 2001, shortly after 10:30 AM, an armed man entered the Zug Parliament chamber while 80 Grand Councillors and the entire cantonal government were gathered. Within two minutes and 34 seconds, Friedrich Leibacher fired 91 shots, killed 14 people and injured 15 others, before taking his own life.
### The raid on the Government Building
Leibacher was 57 years old, a Swiss citizen, had no regular job, and had repeatedly faced legal problems. According to the reconstruction, he acted out of hatred towards the cantonal authorities, having planned the attack alone and well in advance. That morning, he appeared at the Government Building wearing a self-made police vest and a cap with the cantonal coat of arms. He entered the Grand Council chamber, where the session was underway, undisturbed.
He carried a Swiss army assault rifle, a pump-action shotgun, a pistol, a revolver, and a homemade bomb. The source specifies that all weapons had been legally acquired. Leibacher opened fire, shouting insults at the authorities; the deputies sought cover under the benches, and during the attack, he also detonated the explosive device.
The alarm was raised at 10:35 AM. The first responders arrived ten minutes later, at 10:45 AM. 14 ambulances, two Rega helicopters, about a hundred police officers, and 240 firefighters were mobilized to the scene.
### Heinz Tännler's testimony
Heinz Tännler, a member of the UDC and currently the Director of Finance for the canton of Zug, was then sitting near the entrance door. He is the only still-serving member of the government or Parliament who experienced the attack. When Leibacher burst into the room, Tännler threw himself under a bench. Next to him was the liberal-radical deputy Martin Döbeli, severely wounded in the head. Tännler recounted that he could not help him. Döbeli died in the helicopter during transport to the hospital; Tännler, however, sustained minor injuries.
> 'I am not an anxious person. But that day I was afraid. Afraid of dying,' Tännler told the Keystone-ATS agency.
President of the Confederation Moritz Leuenberger spoke of an hour of dismay. In Bern, the President of the National Council, Peter Hess from Zug, prematurely adjourned the session, and the flags on the Federal Palace were lowered to half-mast. On October 1, the day of commemoration in Zug, Switzerland observed a minute of silence; SSR radios and televisions also fell silent. 25 years later, the attack remains the most serious in Swiss history. ## Parliamentary Security: Before and After
The Zug attack led to a noticeable change in the places where elected representatives meet. The source describes a "before" and "after": already on that day, several cantons strengthened controls; subsequently, security gates, alarm buttons, and cameras were introduced. The massacre was not confined to a local emergency but altered the protection of Swiss parliaments.
### From the Federal Palace to the Cantons
The clearest comparison concerns the Federal Palace. Before the attack, it was freely accessible. Afterwards, metal detectors were installed, and baggage screening was introduced. Even today, approximately 100,000 annual visitors must identify themselves and undergo a check. Entry therefore includes identification and baggage screening.
In the cantons, the response was not uniform. Only Appenzell Innerrhoden, among those indicated by the source, did not deem intervention necessary. The measures listed — gates, alarm buttons, and cameras — show a common direction: controlling access, signaling danger, and monitoring spaces. The specifics of the measures, however, depend on cantonal choices.
### Zug and Threat Management
In Zug, for three years following the massacre, the Grand Council met in a protected police building. It then returned to the renovated chamber, with new furnishings and access controls. The reopening was thus accompanied by a modification of the space and entry procedures.
Since 2013, most cantons have implemented a threat management system to identify potentially dangerous individuals in time. Zug does not yet have this system: an amendment to the police law that would introduce it is currently under consultation. The issue thus remains open regarding the transition from physical controls to the proactive assessment of threats.
For the public, the concrete effect is the distinction between free access and regulated access. At the Federal Palace, identification and baggage screening apply; in Zug, the return to the chamber was linked to new controls; in the cantons, threat management systems are not present everywhere in the same way. The source therefore documents a security model built after September 27, 2001.

The source makes it possible to derive a practical sequence for those who need to visit a parliamentary building or follow the evolution of cantonal rules. This is not an identical procedure throughout Switzerland: the measures have changed over time and the cantons have made different choices. The steps list the elements indicated for the Federal Palace and Zug.
### Four useful steps
1. Identify the venue. If the destination is the Federal Palace, bear in mind that the building, once freely accessible, now requires visitors to provide identification and undergo baggage checks. The source indicates approximately 100’000 visitors per year subjected to these checks.
2. Prepare for the entrance check. At the Federal Palace, providing identification and undergoing a baggage check are part of the access procedure described. Cantonal parliaments may also have security gates, alarm buttons and cameras, measures introduced after the massacre.
3. Distinguish the situation in Zug. The Grand Council met for three years in a police-protected building and then returned to the renovated chamber, with new furnishings and access controls. Those following the canton must distinguish the protected venue used during the emergency from the subsequent renovated chamber.
4. Follow the legislative dossier. Since 2013, the majority of cantons have had a threat-management system. Zug does not yet have one; the amendment to the police law that should introduce it is under consultation. For the reader, the operational step is to distinguish between the system already in place in most cantons and the proposal still under consultation in Zug.
This reading avoids confusing three levels: the physical measures at the entrance, the temporary protection of the venue and the threat-management system. The first concerns metal detectors, baggage and identification at the Federal Palace; the second concerns the temporary relocation of the Grand Council of Zug; the third concerns the early identification of potentially dangerous people. These are different elements, even though they belong to the same evolution of parliamentary security.
When reading a cantonal update, the operational criterion is to look for which of the three levels is being modified. In Zug, the return to the renovated chamber concerns the venue; the amendment to the police law concerns the threat-management system. At the Federal Palace, metal detectors, baggage and identification concern access. This distinction makes it possible not to confuse a physical measure with a legislative proposal.

## In brief
- The national projection indicates a 71% no vote. - In Ticino, the no vote stands at 51.2% after 86 municipalities. - In Grisons, no votes reach 66.6%.
## Key facts
- Subject → «Safeguarding Swiss neutrality» - Projection result → rejected by 71% of eligible voters - Promoters → Pro Svizzera and some UDC figures - Projection → gfs.bern on behalf of SSR - Ticino → 51.2% opposed after the count of 86 out of 100 municipalities - Grisons → 66.6% no votes with counting already completed - News source → Keystone-ATS
### The national vote
According to the projection released by gfs.bern on behalf of SSR, 71% of eligible voters rejected the Neutrality Initiative put to a vote today. The news was released by Keystone-ATS. The text was promoted by Pro Svizzera and some UDC figures.
The political scientist from gfs.bern, Urs Bieri, confirmed to Swiss-German-language radio SRF that it would not have been an exciting day. For the expert, the no vote is clear-cut: the initiative received little support outside the right, and it is unclear whether the population understood the issue.
At the regional level, the count produced a distinct picture. In Ticino, after the count of 86 out of 100 municipalities, the text received 51.2% opposition. In Grisons, where the operations had already been completed, the no votes reached 66.6%. These are the two territorial results reported in the source alongside the national projection.
The official name of the text was «Safeguarding Swiss neutrality». The initiative called for making the practice more restrictive by enshrining the permanent and armed character of neutrality in the Constitution. It also called for Bern not to join any military or defense alliance, except in the event of a direct attack.
Another point concerned sanctions: the text sought to renounce sanctions against belligerent states, with the exception of those decided by the UN. The reference point in the debate was the choice adopted, following the European Union, toward Russia after the invasion of Ukraine.
This projection indicates the rejection of the model proposed by Pro Svizzera and UDC figures. The campaign contrasted two interpretations of neutrality: a more rigid one, supported by those in favor, and a flexible one, defended by skeptics and the Federal Council. ## The political scope of the vote
The result concerns a choice of direction for the Confederation: how strict neutrality should be and how much room should remain for foreign policy. The rejected proposal would have enshrined two precise cornerstones in the Constitution — permanent and armed neutrality — and would have limited joining a military or defense alliance to the sole case of a direct attack.
For those who live or work in Switzerland, the concrete issue lies in how the country defines its external relations, not in a personal obligation indicated by the source. The text in fact linked neutrality to Swiss freedom and prosperity, while its opponents pointed to the risk of losing flexibility. The difference can be read as a comparison between written constraints and room for maneuver.
### The comparison between the two approaches
| Reading of neutrality | Political effect indicated in the debate | |---|---| | More restrictive | No military or defense alliance, except in the event of a direct attack; renunciation of sanctions against belligerent states, except those of the UN | | More flexible | Preservation of foreign policy's room for maneuver and of the flexibility considered by many to be the true strength of Swiss neutrality |
Supporters argued that the principle had been emptied of its meaning and shaped to move closer, for example, to NATO. In their view, this represented a danger to the economy and the Confederation's credibility, especially because of its historic role as a mediator.
Skeptics, including the Federal Council, argued the opposite: a new definition would excessively restrict the room for action, with possible damage to security. During the campaign, the text was also described as harmful to security and, by some, as pro-Putin.

### Four useful steps
1. Check the level of the data. The 71% concerns the national projection among eligible voters. The figures for Ticino and Grisons are instead regional results, with different stages of the count. They should not be merged into a single percentage.
2. Read the official title. «Safeguarding Swiss neutrality» identifies the text. From this, the request can be reconstructed: permanent and armed neutrality, no military or defense alliance except in the event of a direct attack, and renunciation of sanctions against belligerent states except those decided by the UN.
3. Compare the rationales. Supporters invoked freedom, prosperity, the economy, credibility and the role of mediator. item.description: The projections on federal initiatives, the vote in Graubünden, and local planning in Poschiavo on September 27, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Neutrality and food: initial projections at 71% and 72% no - Grisons: voting at 16 rejected by 67.42% no - Poschiavo: local plan approved with 56% of the votes
## Key facts - Date → 27 September 2026 - Neutrality, initial projection → 71% no, margin of error 3% - Food, initial projection → 72% no, margin of error 3% - Grisons, voting at 16 → 67.42% no - Grisons, turnout → 45.09% - Poschiavo, local planning → 56%, equal to 850 votes out of 1’621 - Ticino, partial neutrality → 50.29% yes after 52 municipalities - Poschiavo, building plots → from 100 to 82
### The picture emerging from the polls
On 27 September 2026, once voting had closed, the first projections by gfs.bern indicated «no» to the two federal initiatives: 71% for the text on neutrality and 72% for the one on food. The margin of error, plus or minus, was 3%.
The subsequent report put the «no» vote on neutrality at 66.59% and the vote against food at 75.01%. In Ticino, however, neutrality was for the time being approved by 50.29% after the count in 52 of 100 municipalities; the initiative for secure food collected 69.34% no.
In Grisons, the partial revision of the cantonal Constitution on voting from the age of 16 was rejected by 67.42% of voters. None of the 100 municipalities approved the proposal. Buseno, Santa Maria and Cama exceeded 85% no, while turnout stopped at 45.09%. During the partial count in 95 of 100 municipalities, opponents accounted for 68.85%.
The project had been approved by the Grand Council and the Government. Grisons would have become the second Swiss canton to grant voting rights to 16-year-olds, 19 years after the historic Landsgemeinde of Glarona on 6 May 2007. Previously, similar proposals had been rejected in Uri, Basel City, Basel Country, Neuchâtel, Zurich, Bern, Aargau and Lucerne.
### Poschiavo between local plan and new Executive
In Poschiavo, the new local planning, drawn up over a period of 15 years, was approved with 56%: 850 votes out of 1’621. Appeals may be filed within 30 days. The plan reduces building plots from 100 to 82; the cut initially envisaged was 35, but cantonal forecasts proved more favorable. The calculation of compensation for owners of de-zoned land remains to be defined.
Davide Vassella, the only candidate for mayor, was elected after Giovanni Jochum, a Liberal representative. The Socialist who ran on the Poschiavo Viva list obtained 1’076 votes out of 1’575 voters. The municipal council taking office next January will include Fulvio Betti (UDC), Graziano Crameri (AdC), Ruggero Tuena (PLR) and Romano Rossi (AdC); Massimo Tuena, the other Poschiavo Viva candidate, was excluded. ## How to read the results without confusing the different levels
The ballot brings together three different levels on the same day: the federal initiatives on neutrality and food, the revision of the Constitution of the Canton of Grisons, and the municipal decisions of Poschiavo. For the reader, the first practical consequence is to classify each number before interpreting it: a projection on the initiatives, partial cantonal data and a municipal result do not have the same status.
### Projections, partial data and reported result
Moving from estimates to results requires care. The indications from gfs.bern on neutrality and food were projections; the source accompanies them with a margin of error. In what follows, the text reports a more advanced situation for the two federal initiatives and describes the situation in Ticino as provisional: neutrality was narrowly ahead, while food was showing a clear no. The phrase «for now» prevents that passage from being read as a final snapshot.
The Graubünden vote also shows why the counting stage matters. The data released after counting in 95 out of 100 municipalities do not perfectly coincide with the result communicated after the count was completed: the share of opponents falls compared with the partial percentage, while maintaining the same outcome. This is not a contradiction: they are two different moments of the same ballot.
| Level | Element to distinguish | Practical reading | | Federal | Projection and result | Wait for the reported figure | | Grisons | Partial count and final data | Keep the two stages separate | | Poschiavo | Local level and appeals | Take the stated deadline into account |
### The concrete point for Poschiavo
For owners of downzoned land, local planning contains two operational pieces of information: the reduction in building lots and the fact that the calculation of compensation still has to be defined. The deadline for appeals is 30 days. The source does not indicate the amount of compensation, the authority to contact or the documents to attach: adding these details would mean going beyond the available data.

The results of the municipal vote in Bellinzona on the Fortezza project were still awaited, as were the outcomes of various cantonal votes in German-speaking Switzerland and Romandy. item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in the Canton of Solothurn
item.description: Guide to traineeship in the Canton of Solothurn: Swiss framework on minimum wage, hours, holidays, AVS/AI/IPG contributions and taxes.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - No federal minimum wage in Switzerland - Minimum vacation: 5 weeks under 20 years of age - Maximum working hours: 45 or 50 hours per week - OASI/IV/EO: 5.3% employee contribution
## Key facts - Minimum wage → no federal minimum; some Cantons have one - Vacation → 4 weeks minimum; 5 under 20 years - Working hours → 45 hours in specified sectors; 50 in others - OASI/IV/EO → 5.3% employee; 10.6% total - AL/AC → 1.1% up to the annual ceiling - LAMal/KVG → mandatory for residents - Taxes → federal, cantonal, and municipal - Cantons → own legislation and multiplier
The Swiss framework does not provide for a federal minimum wage: some Cantons have their own. For those looking for an apprenticeship and vocational training in the Canton of Solothurn, the distinction already matters when reading the apprentice's remuneration: the national figure is not a single number and the cantonal framework should not be confused with the federal one. The apprenticeship contract and professional baccalaureate are other items to keep separate from general labor rules.
### Working hours, vacation, and remuneration
The maximum working hours indicated by the source are 45 hours per week in industry, offices, and retail, or 50 hours in other sectors. Minimum vacation is four weeks; for those under 20 years old, it rises to five. These are the first references to place alongside the apprenticeship contract, without turning the hour limit into an indication of remuneration.
Salary must also be read together with contributions. Within the OASI/AHV framework, the OASI/IV/EO item is equal to 5.3% for the employee and 10.6% in total with the employer. AL/AC is indicated at 1.1% up to the annual ceiling. Accident insurance (UVG/LAA) varies from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector. Occupational pension (BVG/LPP), on the coordinated salary, provides rates of 7% between 25 and 34 years, 10% between 35 and 44, 15% between 45 and 54, and 18% from 55 years up to the reference age. For an orderly reading of the payslip, the salary calculator can be used alongside the items actually indicated.
The division of responsibilities avoids other misunderstandings. FTA/ESTV deals with direct federal tax and VAT; cantonal administrations manage the cantonal and municipal parts; FSIO/BSV deals with social security, OASI, IV, and occupational pensions, and does not set taxes; FSO/BFS produces statistics and does not establish rates. The real cost of a training path does not coincide with the remuneration alone. For residents, LAMal/KVG is mandatory and must be taken out within three months of arrival. It is a private insurance with per capita premiums: it is not a tax and not a salary contribution. Premiums vary by canton or region, while premium reduction is a cantonal subsidy. For adults, the indicated deductibles are CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, and 2500. This step must be included in the cost of living in Switzerland, especially when the budget starts from an apprenticeship salary.
### Taxation and residency
Taxation follows three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax, and municipal tax. Each Canton has its own law and its own multiplier; the municipality applies a multiplier on the cantonal tax. To evaluate Canton Solothurn, one must therefore separate the federal rule from the cantonal and municipal component. AFC/ESTV deals with IFD and VAT, while cantonal administrations deal with cantonal and municipal taxes. The comparison with the tax return must remain anchored to this structure.
For a foreign person, SEM distinguishes L for short-term stays up to one year, B for renewable residence, C for settlement, normally after 10 years of residence or after 5 for EU/EFTA citizens, and G for cross-border commuters. The category must be identified in the concrete situation.
### Housing and continuity of the relationship
Tenancy follows the federal law of the CO, article 253 and following, the same in every Canton. The security deposit does not exceed three months' rent and goes into a blocked account in the tenant's name. The landlord's notice of termination is valid only on the official cantonal form; the dispute must be submitted within 30 days to the conciliation authority. Within the general framework of work, the source also indicates 14 weeks of maternity leave at 80% via IPG, two weeks of paternity leave, and notice periods of one month in the first year, two from the second to the ninth, and three from the tenth. These items must be separated from the apprenticeship contract and housing costs.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the pension planner and the pillar 3 simulator. ### Selection Checklist
To search for an apprenticeship position in the Canton of Solothurn, it is advisable to create a single profile and update it for each offer. The first field is the pathway: note whether the offer refers to professional training and whether it includes a vocational baccalaureate. For the latter, only note what is written in the offer, without completing the data with extraneous details. For your search, you can start from the job listings, keeping the pathway title and the stated conditions separate.
1. Contract. Read the apprenticeship contract and record the indicated salary, working hours, and vacation. Then compare the hours with the threshold of 45 hours for industry, offices, and retail, or 50 hours in other sectors, and the vacation with the minimum of four weeks or five if under 20 years of age.
2. Payslip. Separate the gross amount from deductions. Use the available rates for AHV/AVS, IV/AI/EO, ALV/AC, UVG/LAINF, and BVG/LPP only to the extent that the item is relevant to the employment relationship; do not add KVG/LAMal, which is a private per capita premium insurance and not a wage contribution. The Swiss payslip helps keep social security separate from health insurance.
3. Residence. If you are a resident, verify the stipulation of KVG/LAMal within three months of arrival. If you are a foreign national, identify the SEM category: L, B, C, or G according to your situation.
4. Housing and taxes. For a rental, check the deposit, the blocked account, and the official form; if you need to contest a landlord's notice to vacate, keep in mind the 30-day deadline before the conciliation authority. For taxes, separate federal tax (IFD), Canton, and municipality, and consider the Canton's law and multiplier. The tax return should be read based on this three-tier structure.
This profile avoids confusing vocational baccalaureate, salary, health insurance, social security, and taxes. For a preliminary estimate of the net salary and the weight of deductions, use the salary calculator.

item.title: Federal votes: neutrality and feeding at the polls
item.description: The Swiss population votes today on neutrality and food. The key data, polls and the position of the federal institutions.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Today, voters are voting on neutrality and food. - Neutrality has 30% support. - The no vote on neutrality is just below 70%. - Self-sufficiency: from 46 to 70% in 10 years.
## Key facts - Votes → neutrality and «For safer food» - Neutrality → «Safeguarding Swiss neutrality» - Signatures collected → over 112'000 - Net self-sufficiency → from 46 to 70% within 10 years - Support for neutrality → around 30% - Support for food → 29% - Proponent → Franziska Herren - Official position → no from the Federal Council
The Swiss population is going to the polls today on two federal initiatives. After the votes on the broadcasting fee and on a Switzerland with 10 million inhabitants, neutrality is once again at the heart of the national debate. The other question concerns food: just hours before the polls close, the ballot thus compares the Confederation’s position with priorities for production, consumption and resources.
### The neutrality proposal
The initiative «Safeguarding Swiss neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)» calls for a more restrictive approach and the inclusion in the Constitution of the concept of permanent and armed neutrality. The Federal Council and Parliament reject it: they argue that the practice followed in this area since 1848 has produced good results and that the current Constitution already provides the room for manoeuvre needed to protect the country’s interests in a changing international framework.
The pro-initiative committee brings together Pro Svizzera and UDC and, in Ticino, also forces from the more radical left, including the Partito Comunista. Supporters argue that international events and the geopolitical crises of recent years have watered down Swiss neutrality, reduced the Confederation’s role as a mediator and the scope of its good offices.
> «The world does not need a Switzerland that does what everyone else does,» said UDC Council of States member Marco Chiesa.
The voting intentions cited by the source show support at around 30%, compared with an opposing camp steady at just under 70% and few undecided voters. The yes vote is concentrated almost exclusively among the UDC base; among the other historic parties, the no vote prevails.
The second question is the initiative «For safer food». Submitted in August two years ago with over 112'000 signatures, it proposes greater consumption and production of plant-based foods, reducing dependence on foreign countries by raising net self-sufficiency from 46 to 70% within 10 years, and stricter measures to protect drinking water, biodiversity and soil fertility. Franziska Herren, the «Acqua pulita per tutti» association and various public figures support the text. The initiative has, however, met with unanimous opposition in both federal chambers; the Federal Council is also opposed. ## Two votes, two possible directions
The most useful way to read the vote is to separate the two questions and their possible effects. The first concerns the Confederation's room for maneuver on neutrality; the second links consumption, food production and resource protection. These are not two overlapping dossiers: both the subject and the type of choice proposed to voters are different.
### Neutrality: what constraint for the Confederation?
If the initiative were to pass, the point sought by its proponents would be permanent and armed neutrality enshrined in the Constitution. For voters, the choice can be understood as a comparison between a stricter rule and the room for maneuver that the Federal Council and Parliament already consider guaranteed by the constitutional text. The reference to practice since 1848 serves the institutional position in defending a path deemed effective; the committee in favor, instead, uses recent geopolitical crises to argue that this practice has been diluted. The vote therefore pits two interpretations of the same neutrality against each other: continuity of practice or its restriction.
The poll also shows a marked difference between the parties. The no vote reaches 76% in the PLR and 94% in the PS, while support in favor remains almost exclusively among the democentrist base. These figures explain why the proposal has been at the center of the national political debate, despite starting from support levels of around 30%.
### Food: contested objective and costs
On the second question, the chain proposed by supporters is precise: reduce the areas devoted to animal feed, increase those for plant foods intended for human consumption, produce more calories and strengthen self-sufficiency. This direction is accompanied by a demand for greater protection of drinking water, biodiversity and soil fertility. Opponents, on the other hand, consider the 70% target unrealistic and fear state intervention in consumption, especially regarding meat and products of animal origin. They also point to the role of livestock farming in mountain regions and the risk of higher prices for Swiss products, resulting in shopping tourism.
The latest Tamedia poll indicates 29% support. Only the Greens' electorate is majority in favor, with 72% yes; the PS and PVL lean toward no, with 52% and 57%, respectively. Centre, UDC and PLR reject the initiative with 82%, 85% and 88% no votes. Among supporters, 30% cite the use of subsidies for sustainable rather than animal production as the main argument; among opponents, 39% fear a menu decided by the state. To follow the daily spending profile referred to in the debate, consult the costo della vita in Svizzera.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## How to reach a decision
### Four steps before the polls close
1. Separate the questions. The first concerns neutrality; the second concerns food supply. Evaluating the two initiatives independently avoids turning a choice on Confederation policy into an automatic response to the agricultural dossier.
2. For neutrality, identify the requested amendment. The text calls for a more restrictive practice and permanent, armed neutrality in the Constitution. The point to weigh is therefore the relationship between this greater rigidity and the margin of manoeuvre that the Federal Council and Parliament already consider available.
3. For food supply, check the three stated objectives: higher consumption and production of plant-based foods, a net self-sufficiency rate from 46 to 70% within 10 years, and stricter measures for drinking water, biodiversity and soil fertility.
4. Compare the possible costs evoked by the two sides. Proponents link the change to lower import dependency, the production of more calories and water protection. Opponents, on the other hand, point to intervention on consumption, the need for livestock farming in mountain regions, rising prices and shopping tourism.
The source places the decision a few hours before the polls close. At this stage, the Tamedia poll can help understand the political climate, but the choice must be brought back to the concrete contents of the two texts: a more restrictive rule on neutrality on one hand, production and resource protection objectives on the other.
Those who want to explore the potential impact of prices on their budget can consult the cost of living in Switzerland. To complete the assessment of your personal budget, use the salary/tax calculator.

item.description: Several thousand people demonstrated in Bern against the tightening of asylum law, calling for fundamental rights and freedom of movement.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Several thousand people demonstrated in Bern - Protest against the tightening of asylum law - Fundamental rights and freedom of movement demanded - Asylum Strategy 2027 and deportation centers in the spotlight
## Key facts - Location → Bern - Participants → several thousand - Organizers → Solidarité sans frontières and around one hundred organizations - Route → from the city center to Federal Square - Slogan → «No borders between us» - Demands → fundamental rights, freedom of movement, and social and political participation
Several thousand people took part today in Bern in a demonstration against the tightening of asylum law and the exclusion of people without Swiss passports. The demonstrators called for fundamental rights to be respected for everyone, without distinctions based on residence status or origin.
The demands also included full freedom of movement and the possibility of participating in social and political life. The march thus linked the asylum debate to the everyday situation of people living in Switzerland without Swiss passports.
### A mobilization supported by many organizations
The demonstration was called by Solidarité sans frontières, an association based in Bern that advocates for asylum and migrants, together with around one hundred other organizations, trade unions, and civil society groups. The march took place under the slogan «No borders between us».
The participants crossed the city center before reaching Federal Square. Along the way, they chanted slogans such as «Long live solidarity without borders», as observed by a reporter from the Keystone-Ats news agency.
In a press release, Solidarité sans frontières spoke of profound changes ahead in migration policy. The association criticized Asylum Strategy 2027, the UDC initiative for border protection, and the reform of the Common European Asylum System.
The flyer distributed during the demonstration read: «We defend our fundamental rights against authoritarian tendencies». The organizers described migration as a normal phenomenon that existed in the past and is set to continue. They also called for an open and diverse society, urging people not to let themselves be divided.
The final part of the demands concerns deportations, regularization, and the immediate closure of detention centers for deportation. According to the demonstrators, the fundamental rights to be guaranteed to everyone include access to healthcare, education, and work, as well as legal protection regardless of residence status. For those living in Switzerland, the practical point of the demonstration lies in the distinction between the political demands and the rules actually described by the source. The text does not present a new procedure, indicate a deadline or specify which provisions have already changed. Instead, it reports the protesters’ positions on a possible evolution of migration policy.
The first issue concerns the criterion by which rights should be assessed: the organizers demand that they be recognized for all people, regardless of residence status or origin. The second concerns freedom of movement, presented as an alternative to borders. The third touches on participation in social and political life. Taken together, these demands broaden the issue beyond the asylum procedure alone.
### What changes in the reading of the proposals
The statement places the 2027 asylum strategy, the UDC initiative for border protection and the reform of the Common European Asylum System on the same level of discussion. The source, however, does not explain the specific content of these measures or indicate which authority should apply them. For this reason, it does not allow permits, forms, deadlines or individual effects to be inferred.
The same applies to the rights listed in the flyer. Access to healthcare, education and work is indicated by the protesters as a fundamental right to be guaranteed, but no conditions, procedures or necessary documents are provided. The reference to work contains no data on wages, sectors or available positions; for an operational link, it is possible to consult annunci di lavoro, keeping the job search separate from the political demands of the demonstration.
A reader wishing to assess possible developments must therefore separate three elements: the fact of the protest, the organizers’ demands and the political changes that the latter are contesting. If a measure on one of these issues were adopted in the future, its effect would have to be verified in the specific text of the measure. The source does not make it possible to say today whether the freedom of movement, social participation, access to services or legal protection of a particular person would change.
This distinction prevents a demand from the streets from being turned into an already applicable rule. The content of the demonstration is political and concerns the direction of migration policy; it does not, however, offer individual administrative guidance.

To read the news usefully, one can follow a simple sequence based exclusively on the elements reported by the source. The process serves to distinguish what happened in Bern from the demands put forward by the organizers and the political interventions criticized.
### Five practical steps
1. Start with the verifiable fact: a demonstration with several thousand participants took place in Bern, organized by Solidarité sans frontières together with other organizations, trade unions and civil society groups.
2. Identify the issue that concerns you. The source mentions residence status, origin, freedom of movement, participation in social and political life, access to healthcare, education and work, and legal protection.
